rules.preview:
# Alex's global preferences

- Be direct. Say what you changed and why in a few lines, not an essay.
- Never run destructive git commands (reset --hard, clean -fd, push --force) without asking.
- Prefer small commits with a one line subject in the imperative mood.
- When a test fails, show the failing assertion before you change anything.
- Do not add dependencies without saying why.

# aurora-docs

React docs site with an OpenAPI 3.1 viewer. pnpm, Vite, vitest, Playwright.

- Unit tests: `pnpm test`; end to end: `pnpm e2e` (starts the dev server itself).
- The interactive API playground must work without JavaScript errors on plain HTTP previews.
- Keep 4.5:1 contrast on every badge and button, in both themes.
- Do not reformat generated files under `src/openapi/generated`.

# nexus-gateway

Rust workspace. Gateway hot path: be careful with allocations.

- Test: `cargo test --workspace`; lint: `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`.
- The token bucket rate limiter lives in `crates/limiter`; its public API is frozen.
- Prefer `Instant` injection over reading the clock inside limiter code.
- Benchmarks in `benches/` must be run with `--release`.
- Terraform under `deploy/` is production: plan only, never apply from an agent.

# skyline-weather

TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL. Package manager: pnpm.

- Test: `pnpm test` (vitest, files sit next to the source).
- The Doppler radar sweep clock must never wait on the network; tile refresh runs beside it.
- Every new radar function gets a fake-timer test, no real sleeps.
- Do not touch `src/ingest/config.ts` defaults without checking the staging poller.
- Commit style: `radar: ...`, `alerts: ...`, `ingest: ...`.

# vortex-pipeline

Rust plus Python. The parquet zero-copy deserializer is the hot path.

- Rust tests: `cargo test --workspace --release` (debug is too slow for the fixtures).
- Python tests: `cd py/ingest && pytest -q`.
- Never allocate per chunk in `crates/reader`; reuse the scratch buffer.
- Schema changes need a migration in `migrations/` and a test.

# zenith-cli

Rust CLI built with clap. Output goes through `src/output`.

- Test: `cargo test`; integration tests in `tests/`.
- Every command that prints must support `--format json`.
- Keep the distributed consensus ping read only; it never changes cluster state.
- Errors are `anyhow::Result` at the edge, typed errors inside `src/consensus.rs`.

# Codex defaults

- Ask before running anything that touches the network or production configs.
- Keep patches small; one concern per patch.
- Run the project's test command before saying a change works.
- No dependency changes unless asked.

# aurora-docs agents

- Install with `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`.
- Test: `pnpm test`, e2e: `pnpm e2e`.
- Accessibility changes need an axe check in the same PR.

# nexus-gateway agents

Rust workspace.

- Test: `cargo nextest run --workspace` (falls back to `cargo test`).
- Format: `cargo fmt --all` before every commit.
- Production routing config is read only for agents.

# skyline-weather agents

TypeScript web app. Package manager: npm (the CI image has no pnpm).

- Test: `npm test`
- Lint: `npm run lint`, type check: `npm run typecheck`
- Keep PRs under 300 changed lines.
- Local mock feed: `./scripts/test_radar_feed.sh` (needs the mock on :8089).
- export RADAR_TOKEN=[masked] # local mock only

# vortex-pipeline agents

- Rust: `cargo test --workspace --release`.
- Python: `pytest -q` in `py/ingest`.
- Profile with `--features dhat-heap` before claiming a speed up.

# zenith-cli agents

- Test: `cargo test`; lint: `cargo clippy -- -D warnings`.
- Do not add new dependencies without a note in the PR.

# Gemini defaults

- Explain the plan in two or three bullets before editing.
- Prefer reading files over guessing.
- Do not rewrite files you were not asked to touch.

# aurora-docs (Gemini)

Docs site. Search index is built by `scripts/build-search-index.ts`.

# nexus-gateway (Gemini)

Audit before editing: list the files you will change. gRPC settings are in `crates/grpc`.

# skyline-weather (Gemini)

Read `src/radar` before suggesting changes to the sweep. Tests: `npm test`.

# vortex-pipeline (Gemini)

Measure first. Use the `batch_profile` binary for allocation numbers.

# zenith-cli (Gemini)

Cluster admin CLI. Fixtures for tests are in `tests/fixtures`.

blocks.text: We're moving the limiter's Redis from the single primary to the new 6-node cluster. Set up connection pooling for the token bucket rate limiter against the cluster. I'd guess 16 connections per replica, tell me if that's wrong. Seed nodes will come from LIMITER_REDIS_NODES.
I'll check the limiter's dependencies and where it builds its pool today.

The limiter builds a single-node `deadpool_redis` pool in `RedisBucket::connect`. I'll enable the cluster features, put pool construction in its own module, and switch `connect` to take seed nodes. 16 is reasonable: a cluster connection multiplexes to every shard, so you need far fewer than the 64 a single node pool used.

blocks.text:
Done, with one decision worth checking. The schema migration of the stored keys is deliberately not a data migration:

- **Old keys are left to expire.** Each bucket key carries a TTL of twice its full-refill time, so every `bucket:*` key disappears by itself within minutes.
- **No `RENAME`.** On a cluster `RENAME` fails with `CROSSSLOT` when the old and new key hash to different slots, which they will. A read-through copy is not worth it for counters that refill in seconds.
- **Cost:** during the rolling deploy, replicas on the old build and the new build use different keys, so a client can briefly get double its budget. Seconds to minutes, then it settles.

Also changed: `RedisBucket::connect` now takes `&[String]` seed nodes, and `tests/redis_atomic.rs` was updated to match. I ran `cargo check` and the key unit test; I did not run anything against a real cluster, so the 16-connection figure is a reasoned starting point and not a measurement.
ok, give me the rollout notes for ops

Rollout notes:

1. Set `LIMITER_REDIS_NODES` on every replica to a comma separated list of seed URLs (three of the six is plenty; the client discovers the rest).
2. Deploy normally. Expect a short window of mixed `bucket:*` and `rl:v2:*` keys, and slightly generous limits during it.
3. Afterwards, `redis-cli --cluster call <seed> scan 0 match 'bucket:*'` should drain to empty within a few minutes. If it does not, a replica is still on the old build.
4. Watch connection counts per replica; if they sit pinned at 16, raise `DEFAULT_POOL_SIZE` in `crates/limiter/src/pool.rs`.

Rollback is safe: the old build reads the old keys, which simply start empty (full buckets).

The ASAN job in CI is red on main: heap-buffer-overflow, READ of size 8, in I64Dict::from_page. The corrupt-page fixture has a dictionary header claiming 268M values on a 4 KB page and we just trust it. Add proper bounds checks for dictionary pages in the parquet zero-copy deserializer, with tests. Don't just change the fixture.
I'll look at every caller of `from_page` and at the current implementation.

The bug is in `from_page`: it builds a slice of `num_values` i64s straight from the header without comparing against `page.len()`. I'll add a `DictPageTruncated` error, compute the byte count with `checked_mul` so a huge count can't wrap, and use `align_to` on exactly that many bytes instead of `from_raw_parts`. Then tests for the oversized header and for an exact fit.

does buildCurl drop the body for GET like the widget does? just answer, no edits

Yes, it is the same function the widget uses. `buildCurl` only appends `--data-raw` when the method is not `GET` or `HEAD`, so a leftover body on a GET never reaches the command. The playground also passes `undefined` for GET before calling it, so it is covered twice.

For the new button:

- the component test checks the exact string written to the clipboard for a POST with a body, and the one snapshot now includes the extra button

One gap: the command does not include the signing headers or any custom headers the Headers tab might gain later, because that tab is still a static line of text.

Fixed. The limiter tests pass (10 of 10, including the new regression test) and clippy is clean with `-D warnings`.

**Root cause:** `Limiter::merge_remote` computed `min(local, remote) + pending_refund` and stored it without the capacity clamp that `Bucket::refill` applies. After a long idle gap the bucket was already full, so any pending refund pushed it past the burst. Only replicas that sync with Redis call `merge_remote`, which is why single replicas looked fine.

```rust
let merged = self.tokens.min(remote_tokens) + self.pending_refund;
self.tokens = merged.min(self.capacity as f64);
```

The public API did not change. One thing I did not touch: `refund` itself still lets `pending_refund` grow without bound if `merge_remote` is never called on a replica. That is harmless now that the merge clamps, but a cap there would be tidier if you want it as a follow-up.

log = logging.getLogger("vortex.ingest")


class TokenBucket:
    '''Token bucket: refills `rate` rows per second, holds at most `burst` rows.'''

    def __init__(self, rate: float, burst: float, clock=time.monotonic, sleep=time.sleep):
        if rate <= 0 or burst <= 0:
            raise ValueError("rate and burst must be positive")
        self.rate = rate
        self.burst = burst
        self._clock = clock
        self._sleep = sleep
        self._tokens = burst
        self._stamp = clock()
        self._lock = threading.Lock()

    def acquire(self, n: int) -> float:
        '''Block until `n` rows may be sent. Returns the seconds spent waiting.'''
        n = min(n, self.burst)  # a request bigger than the bucket would never be satisfied
        waited = 0.0
        while True:
            with self._lock:
                now = self._clock()
                self._tokens = min(self.burst, self._tokens + (now - self._stamp) * self.rate)
                self._stamp = now
                if self._tokens >= n:
                    self._tokens -= n
                    return waited
                wait = (n - self._tokens) / self.rate
            self._sleep(wait)
            waited += wait

def __init__(self, ring: RingClient, schema: EventSchema, batch_rows: int = 4096, workers: int = 4,
                 rows_per_s: float | None = None):

        self.batch_rows = batch_rows
        self.workers = workers
        self.dropped = 0

        self.limiter = TokenBucket(rows_per_s, burst=batch_rows) if rows_per_s else None

blocks.text: what happens if a batch is bigger than the burst?

It is clamped: `acquire` does `n = min(n, self.burst)`, so an oversized batch waits for one full burst to refill instead of waiting forever for tokens the bucket can never hold. The cost is that a batch of 10,000 rows is billed as 4,096 if the burst is 4,096, so the real rate can run above `rows_per_s` in that case. Setting `burst` to at least the batch size avoids it, which is what `Producer` does (`burst=batch_rows`).

What changed in `py/ingest/producer.py`:

- New `TokenBucket(rate, burst, clock, sleep)` with `acquire(n)`, guarded by a lock because the encoder pool calls it from several threads.
- `Producer(..., rows_per_s=None)`: when set, `run()` calls `self.limiter.acquire(batch.num_rows)` before each `ring.push`.

```python
if self.limiter:
    self.limiter.acquire(batch.num_rows)
```

The four tests in `ingest/tests/test_ratelimit.py` cover the free first burst, the wait for a refill, the clamp and bad arguments. I only ran the unit tests, not the backfill job itself, so the right `rows_per_s` for production still needs picking from how fast the sink drains.

blocks.text: batches are showing up at the sink out of order. the dashboard says seq 4118 landed before 4116 on the orders topic, and it started after we raised the producer workers to 4 for the backfill. trace why: is it the producer, the ring buffer or the sink? Don't change anything yet, I just want the cause.
I'll follow `seq` end to end: where it is assigned, how it moves through the ring, and where the sink complains.

The ring is a plain FIFO: `try_push` writes at `tail`, `try_pop` reads at `head`, so it can't reorder anything. The sink only reports what it sees. The suspicious line is in the producer: `seq` is assigned when a chunk is submitted, but `run` pushes in `as_completed` order, which is the order the encoder threads finish. I'll reproduce that with a fake ring and randomised encode times, without touching the real code.

import random, time

from ingest.schema import EventSchema

    def __init__(self):
        self.seqs = []
    def push(self, b):
        self.seqs.append(b.seq)


ring = Ring()
p = Producer(ring, EventSchema.default(), batch_rows=10, workers=4)

blocks.text:
Found it, and nothing was changed.

**Cause:** `Producer.run` in `py/ingest/producer.py` submits every chunk to a `ThreadPoolExecutor` with `seq` assigned in submission order, then pushes with `for fut in as_completed(futures)`. `as_completed` yields futures in the order they finish. With `workers=4` a slow batch (more variable string columns, so slower to encode) is overtaken by later, faster ones. With 1 worker the two orders are identical, which is why it only began after the worker count went up.

**Evidence:** a fake ring with random 0 to 10 ms encode times gives 71 inversions in 200 batches, such as seq 2 pushed before seq 1. Neither the ring (FIFO by construction) nor the sink (`SeqGuard::observe` only reports the gap) reorders anything.

**Fix I'd suggest:** keep encoding in parallel but push in `seq` order with a bounded window of in-flight futures. That also stops `run` from materialising a future for every chunk of a big backfill up front.

Taking the oldest future first, with a window of `2 * workers` in flight. The rate limiter and the `RingFull` handling move into a small `_push` so both loops share them.

blocks.text: Review the Doppler radar sweep fragment shader for performance. Users on integrated GPUs report the radar dropping to about 40 fps when zoomed out, where 165k points overlap. Apply the safe changes, list the rest.
Reading the shader, and where its uniforms are set, to separate what I can change in the GLSL alone from what needs TypeScript.

Three things in the fragment stage are costing you at 165k overlapping points: a data-dependent loop and branch in `rampColor`, a `pow()` with a fractional exponent, and a `discard`. On tile-based mobile and integrated GPUs `discard` also disables early depth/stencil rejection, and here the alpha already goes to zero at the edge. Fixing those three in the shader only.

blocks.text: good. write up the rest as a list I can paste into the issue

Applied in `sweep.frag.glsl` (no TypeScript changes needed):

- `rampColor` is now four clamped `mix` calls with no loop and no branch. The result is identical to the old piecewise interpolation for every `v`.
- `pow(x, 1.6)` became `x * x * (1.5 - 0.5 * x)`, a maximum error of 0.0243 before the 0.85 alpha scale (checked over 10,001 samples), about 5 of 255 output levels at worst. Look at the soft edge on a real screen to judge whether that is visible.
- The `discard` is gone; alpha is 0 outside the disc anyway.

Not applied, for the issue:

1. **Bake the ramp into a 256x1 texture.** One `texture2D` fetch replaces four divides and four mixes. Needs `RadarSweep.ts` to build the texture from `VELOCITY_STOPS` and bind a sampler.
2. **Move `sin(u_time * 3.0 + v_velocity * 12.0)` to the vertex shader.** It is per-fragment today although `v_velocity` is constant per point; a varying `v_flicker` would make it per-vertex.
3. **Precompute the segment spans as uniforms** (`u_invSpan[4]`) so the four divides disappear if the texture route is not taken.
4. **Measure with a GPU timer query, not frame rate.** I have not profiled on hardware, so the 40 fps figure and any gain are unconfirmed. `EXT_disjoint_timer_query` is not available on every browser.

-- Atomic token bucket. One round trip, so replicas can never interleave a read and a write.
-- KEYS[1]  bucket key (hash with fields tokens, ts)
-- ARGV[1]  capacity (tokens)
-- ARGV[2]  refill rate (tokens per second)
-- ARGV[3]  tokens requested
-- Returns {allowed (0 or 1), remaining tokens as a string}

local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[1])
local refill = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local want = tonumber(ARGV[3])

-- Use the Redis clock, not the caller's, so replicas with skewed clocks agree.
local t = redis.call('TIME')
local now = t[1] * 1000 + math.floor(t[2] / 1000)

local state = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(state[1])
local ts = tonumber(state[2])
if tokens == nil then
  tokens = capacity
  ts = now
end

local elapsed = math.max(0, now - ts)
tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + (elapsed / 1000) * refill)

local allowed = 0
if tokens >= want then
  tokens = tokens - want
  allowed = 1
end

redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 'tokens', tostring(tokens), 'ts', now)
-- A full bucket is indistinguishable from a missing key, so let idle buckets expire.
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], math.ceil(capacity / refill) * 1000 * 2)
return {allowed, tostring(tokens)}

**Retry segment uploads with exponential backoff**

- `flush_segment` now retries an object store put when it fails with `StoreError::Timeout`: up to 5 attempts, waiting 200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms, 1.6 s between them (base doubles each time, capped at 10 s). Any other store error still fails on the first try.
- The attempt the upload succeeded on is passed to `ManifestClient::record`, which fills `segment_manifest.write_attempts` (the column added by the 0014 schema migration). Previously it was always `1`.
- `RetryPolicy` is configurable through `SegmentWriter::with_retry`; the default is what is described above.

```rust
pub fn backoff(&self, attempt: u16) -> Duration {
    let exp = self.base.saturating_mul(1u32 << (attempt - 1).min(16));
    exp.min(self.cap)
}
```

Tests (paused tokio clock, so no real sleeping): `retries_timeouts_with_backoff` fails 3 puts then succeeds and checks both the store saw 4 attempts and the manifest row says 4; `gives_up_after_max_attempts` checks it stops at 5 and returns the store error.

Left out on purpose: jitter. With one writer per partition I don't expect retries to line up, but if several sinks share a store it is a one-line addition in `backoff`.

validate that the rate limiter's atomic increments hold up under contention. 16 threads, one shared bucket, and check the allowed/denied counters add up to the number of attempts. use release mode, debug hides this stuff
I'll read the counters first, then write a contention test that drains a bucket with no refill so the expected totals are exact.

The test caught a genuine bug. `Stats::record` does `load` then `store(current + 1)`, which is a read-modify-write that is not atomic: two threads read the same value and both write back `current + 1`, losing an increment. In this run about 270 allowed increments went missing out of 10,000. `fetch_add` makes it one atomic operation.

The counters were not atomic and are now. Summary:

- **Found:** `Stats::record` in `crates/limiter/src/stats.rs` lost updates under contention (9,731 of 10,000 allowed calls counted).
- **Fixed:** replaced the load/store pair with `fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed)`.
- **Added:** `crates/limiter/tests/contention.rs`, 16 threads by 2,000 attempts on one bucket, asserting exactly 10,000 allowed and that allowed plus denied equals 32,000.

The token bucket itself was fine: it sits behind a `Mutex`, so exactly 10,000 calls succeeded.
is Relaxed enough there or should those be SeqCst?

`Relaxed` is enough. The two counters are independent, nothing else synchronises on their values, and `fetch_add` is atomic at any ordering, so no increment can be lost. `SeqCst` would only add a stronger global ordering that nobody observes here.

One thing `Relaxed` does not give you: a reader that loads `allowed()` and then `denied()` can see them from slightly different moments, so a ratio computed from the two is approximate while traffic is flowing. For a metrics endpoint that is normal. If a consumer needs a consistent pair, pack both into one `AtomicU64` (32 bits each) and read it once.

```rust
counter.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed);
```

The test only ran on this machine in release mode, so it shows the lost update is gone, not that it cannot happen on weaker memory models.

- [ ] Document the schema in docs/health-schema.md

## Order of work

1. JSON first: everything else builds on the same `HealthReport` struct.
2. Prometheus is a different rendering of the same struct, no new probes.

add RateLimit-Remaining and Retry-After headers to responses from the token bucket rate limiter middleware. Retry-After only on the 429.
I'll look at the middleware and what the bucket can already report.

The bucket only exposes `try_acquire`, so I'll add `remaining()` and `retry_after()` to it, then set the headers in the middleware: `Retry-After` (rounded up to whole seconds) on the 429, `RateLimit-Remaining` on successful responses.
Both headers are in. A successful response now carries `RateLimit-Remaining` (whole tokens left after this request) and a 429 carries `Retry-After` in whole seconds, rounded up.
should Retry-After round up? and what happens for a route with no refill

Yes, round up. If the bucket needs 1.2 s for the next token and the header says 1, a client that obeys it retries 0.2 s early and gets another 429, which then restarts its backoff. Rounding up costs a client at most one extra second.

For a route with `refill_per_s = 0`, `retry_after` returns `Duration::MAX` instead of dividing by zero (which would panic in `Duration::from_secs_f64`). The header then carries an enormous number of seconds, which is technically honest, since that bucket never refills. If you would rather omit the header in that case, it is a one-line check in the middleware; I did not add a test for it, only for the normal path.

Yes, it is shared, and a 429 now slows everyone down.

- `fetchForecast` takes an optional `limiter` and defaults to one module-level `RateLimiter(8, 4)`, so `poller.ts` and `ForecastChart.tsx` draw from the same bucket.
- On a 429 the request calls `limiter.penalize(delay)`, which blocks every queued `acquire()` until that delay has passed. Other retryable statuses (502, 503, 504) only back off the request that saw them.
- `Retry-After` accepts seconds or an HTTP date; it was returning raw seconds at first and the test caught it.
- New test: a second location requested during the pause does not reach `fetch` until the pause is over.

```ts
const delay = backoffDelay(attempt, parseRetryAfter(res.headers.get("retry-after")));
if (res.status === 429) limiter.penalize(delay);
await sleep(delay);
```
